findings.finding: The plan locates the `claim --review` logic 'at the claim.py:133 seam' — which is inside `claim_compute` — but never clarifies whether `--review` is implemented as a new parameter on `claim_compute` or as pre-call logic in `claim_cli`. If placed in `claim_cli` instead, no parameter threading is needed and the cascade invariant is trivially preserved. The current description creates implementation ambiguity: an implementer who puts the LLM call inside `claim_compute`'s body without a guarding parameter could inadvertently make the cascade path also trigger a review, or could add the parameter but forget to document the cascade-omission as intentional. The Scope section omits `claim_cli` as a changed function (lists only `claim.py`), further suggesting the intended seam is inside `claim_compute`, which needs clarification.

Importing a private exit-code mapper with side-effects from _cli into _commands entangles a command-layer module with CLI presentation concerns — if _disposition_exit_code is worth sharing, the plan should either inline the ~3-line mapping in the two _commands call sites or extract it to a shared, layer-neutral location (e.g. rebar._commands._seam or rebar.llm.plan_review).
findings.location: Approach section — 'map the returned verdict dict to the process exit status via _cli._llm_commands._disposition_exit_code(result, indeterminate_code=2)'
scenarios: When a future refactor moves or renames _disposition_exit_code (it is private), _commands/composer.py and _commands/claim.py silently break.
When _commands modules are imported without the full _cli stack (e.g. in library use or unit tests that stub _cli), the import of _cli._llm_commands pulls in argparse and other CLI-only dependencies.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC clause (or extend AC2) explicitly stating that a BLOCK verdict from `edit --review` leaves the EDIT event committed and does not roll it back.
evidence: Testing: 'a BLOCK leaves the edit committed'
AC2 covers only call order and exit codes (PASS/BLOCK/INDETERMINATE), not the committed-edit guarantee
ABSENCE: no AC states 'on BLOCK, the previously committed EDIT event is not rolled back'
findings.finding: The Testing section asserts 'a BLOCK leaves the edit committed' as a behavioral guarantee, but no Acceptance Criterion covers or verifies this property.
findings.location: Testing section; AC2 (edit --review)
scenarios: An operator or downstream tool relying on edit --review for a best-effort commit-then-review workflow has no contractual guarantee that a BLOCK verdict won't be misread as a failure that rolls back the edit.
findings.suggested_fix: Append to AC2: 'a BLOCK verdict leaves the preceding EDIT event committed and does not roll it back (checked: unit test asserting the event store contains the EDIT event after a BLOCK stub)'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add or update an ADR documenting the --review in-verb verification pattern, the rejected fused-verb alternative, the PASS/BLOCK/INDETERMINATE control-flow contract, and the MCP surface exclusion, so the architectural decision is preserved for future maintainers.
evidence: Plan states 'Alternative rejected: new fused verbs — no OSS precedent, larger surface' — a documented design choice with explicit trade-off reasoning, exactly what an ADR captures.
Plan references 'ADR 0040' for the exit-code convention, showing ADRs are used in this project, but creates no ADR for the new --review pattern.
Scope lists composer.py, claim.py, help texts, docs/exit-codes.md, tests — no ADR file appears.
findings.finding: The plan introduces a novel in-verb verification pattern (--review flags that run LLM review inside edit/claim) and explicitly rejects an alternative (new fused verbs), but no ADR is planned to capture this architectural decision. Both T7 and T5e require a novel architectural decision to be captured in an ADR or design doc.
findings.location: Approach section (design rationale); Scope section (no ADR listed); AC section (no ADR assertion)
scenarios: A future engineer sees --review in claim.py, doesn't understand why it bypasses the fused-verb approach, and re-opens the rejected alternative.
The MCP fence (REBAR_MCP_ALLOW_LLM) boundary decision is undocumented in any architecture record.
findings.suggested_fix: Create docs/adr/NNNN-review-flags.md (following the project's existing ADR format implied by ADR 0040) covering: context (edit-then-re-review hazard), decision (embed verification in consuming verb, not new fused commands), consequences (exit-code contract, lock discipline, MCP exclusion), and rejected alternative (new fused verbs).

gates.py is not listed in Scope, so the recovery text is not scheduled for update.

findings.finding: The existing recovery text at src/rebar/_commands/gates.py:213-215 currently tells users to 'run review-plan then claim by hand' — after this change that instruction becomes stale/misleading because claim --review automates exactly that flow, but the plan does not say this text will be updated.
findings.location: Context section: 'claim's recovery text (src/rebar/_commands/gates.py:213-215) tells the user to run review-plan then claim by hand'; Scope section (gates.py not listed)
scenarios: After the change is shipped, a user blocked by the claim gate reads the recovery text, follows the old manual instructions instead of using claim --review, and wonders why the flag exists.
findings.suggested_fix: In gates.py recovery text, replace the manual instruction with: 'Re-run with `rebar claim <id> --review` to review and claim in one step, or run `rebar review-plan <id>` then `rebar claim <id>` manually.'
